overview: Heligan has a story that makes the gardens far more interesting than a pretty day out. The Tremayne family laid them out on the hill above Mevagissey between the 1700s and the early 1900s, but after the First World War, when so many of the gardeners went off to fight, the place was left to go wild and disappeared under brambles. It was rediscovered and brought back to life in the 1990s.

There’s a lot of it: over 200 acres, from tidy, working kitchen gardens near the house to steep, jungly valleys running down towards the sea, plus woodland and a farm. It’s almost all outdoors and much of it is on slopes, so wear shoes you can walk in and bring a waterproof just in case.

expect.title: The productive gardens
expect.text: Flower and vegetable gardens are still kept productive, much as they would have been in Victorian times. Hunt out the pineapple pit, heated by rotting manure, where gardeners managed to grow pineapples in Cornwall.

expect.title: The Jungle
expect.text: A deep, sheltered valley packed with subtropical tree ferns and bamboo that feels a world away from the rest of Cornwall. Children tend to love it.

expect.title: The Mud Maid and Giant’s Head
expect.text: Two big figures sculpted from rock, earth and plants are tucked away along the woodland walks. Make finding them a mission.

expect.title: Woods and farm animals
expect.text: Beyond the gardens are around 60 acres of woodland and meadows, and a farm with traditional and rare breeds of animals and poultry.

expect.title: Seasonal events
expect.text: Guided walks and workshops run through the year, and on selected winter evenings there’s a lantern-lit night garden trail with its own tickets.

goodToKnow.label: Opening
goodToKnow.text: Open every day. Booking ahead is a good idea, for day tickets and local passes alike.

goodToKnow.label: Tickets
goodToKnow.text: Entry is paid. Cornwall and Devon residents can get a locals’ pass, and there are annual passes if you’ll be back.

goodToKnow.label: Food
goodToKnow.text: The Heligan Kitchen restaurant cooks with meat and produce from the estate, and does Sunday roasts.

goodToKnow.label: Where it is
goodToKnow.text: About 2.5 km north-west of Mevagissey, and roughly 10 km by road from St Austell and its station.

entry.note: Paid entry, with locals’ and annual passes

week.text: Heligan suits a dry or showery day on the south coast. Give it a good half day so you’re not rushing the Jungle, then drop down into Mevagissey for the harbour and something to eat, or head for the beach at Pentewan.

pairWith.why: a busy fishing harbour just down the hill
the other big garden day out, if you want to compare

tips: Start with the Jungle while legs are fresh: the climb back up is the hardest part of the visit.
Pack a waterproof; there’s little cover once you’re out in the valleys.
